throughout lactation, with a 10% contribution from LCPUFA in the n-6 and n-3 series to these ranges. The ratio of n-6: n-3 unsat-
urated fatty acids in the diet is important because these fatty acids are desaturated and elongated, and incorporated into membranes,
using the same series of enzymes. Increased intake of linoleic acid reduces the conversion of a-linolenic acid to EPA and DHA,
whereas the conversion of linoleic acid to arachidonic acid is inhibited by EPA and DHA, as well as by arachidonic acid, a-linolenic
acid, and linoleic acid itself. The n-6:n-3 ratio recommended for adults by both DRI and FAO/WHO committees is 5:1 to 10:1. Vege-
table oils are the main dietary source of n-6 fatty acids, and also of n-3 fatty acids although in lower amounts. Fish such as herring,
mackerel, and salmon are good sources of n-3 fatty acids.
The intake of trans fatty acids (trans isomers of oleic and linoleic acid) present in hydrogenated food fats and oils, deep-fried
foods, and meats are of special concern during lactation when intake is excessively high, or when EFA intake is low during pregnancy
and lactation. An inverse correlation of arachidonic acid and DHA with trans fatty acids in plasma lipids has been reported in
infants, suggesting impaired LCPUFA synthesis and metabolism.
